text: Proof. Reductions. For \(G\) as in the second statement, \(\bar G=G/\gamma_5(G)\) is nilpotent with finite abelianization, hence finite; its lower central factors are images of tensor powers of \(\bar G_{ab}\), so \(\bar G\) is a \(3\)-group, and \(D_5(G)\subseteq\gamma_5(G)\) follows from \(D_5(\bar G)=1\) by functoriality. So let \(Q\) be a finite \(3\)-group with \(\gamma_5(Q)=1\) and \(Q/\gamma_2\) of exponent \(3\); we show \(D_5(Q)=1\). Tahara's Theorem 6.1 is stated for any finite group with an \(N\)-series ending at \(H_5=1\) [Tah81, §6, p. 159], so class \(\le3\) needs no separate treatment. We write \(\gamma_3\) and \(\gamma_4\) additively where convenient.

text: Identities. (i) \(\gamma_2/\gamma_3\), \(\gamma_3/\gamma_4\), \(\gamma_4\) are elementary abelian: they are spanned by the values of bilinear maps with one argument in \(Q/\gamma_2\). (ii) \(P\colon Q/\gamma_2\to\gamma_2/\gamma_3\), \(x\mapsto x^3\gamma_3\), and \(\pi\colon\gamma_2/\gamma_3\to\gamma_3/\gamma_4\), \(a\mapsto a^3\gamma_4\), are homomorphisms. (iii) For \(x\in Q\), \(a\in\gamma_2\): \[[x^3,a]=[x,a]^3=[x,a^3],\qquad [a,x^3]=[a,x]^3.\] Indeed, for \(c=[x,a]\in\gamma_3\), \(c^x=c[c,x]\) with \([c,x]\) central, so \([x^3,a]=c^3[c,x]^3=c^3\) as \(\gamma_4\) has exponent \(3\); and \([x,a^3]=c\,c^a c^{a^2}=c^3\) as \([\gamma_3,\gamma_2]=1\). Consequently, if \(a\in\gamma_2\) and \(a^3\in\gamma_4\), then \([x^3,a]=[x,a^3]=1\).

text: Tahara's description. Choose bases of uniqueness: \(x_1,\dots,x_s\) of \(Q/\gamma_2\) such that \(x_1,\dots,x_m\) span a complement of \(\ker P\) and \(x_{m+1},\dots,x_s\) span \(\ker P\) (so \(x_i^3\in\gamma_3\) for \(i>m\)); \(x_{2k}=x_k^3\) for \(k\le m\), completed to a basis \(x_{21},\dots,x_{2t}\) of \(\gamma_2/\gamma_3\). All orders \(d(i),e(k),f(l)\) equal \(3\), and the constants \(b_{ik}\) of \(x_i^3\equiv\prod_k x_{2k}^{b_{ik}}\pmod{\gamma_3}\) are \(b_{ik}=\delta_{ik}\) for \(i\le m\), \(b_{ik}=0\) for \(i>m\). By [Tah81, Thm. 6.1] (checked against the original, pp. 159–161), \(D_5(Q)\) is generated by the elements \[g=\sum_{i<j}u_{ij}[x_i^3,x_j]+\sum_{i,k}v_{ik}\sum_{l>k}b_{il}[x_{2l},x_{2k}]+\sum_{i\le j\le k}w_{ijk}[x_i^3,x_j,x_k]\] for integer families \((u,v,v',w,w',w'')\) satisfying Tahara's conditions (A)–(F) (Tahara writes \(g\) with minus signs; the conditions are homogeneous, so the subgroup is the same). With all orders \(3\) we use: (B) \(\sum_{h>i}u_{ih}b_{hk}-\sum_{h<i}u_{hi}b_{hk}+3v_{ik}+3v'_{ik}=0\); (C) \(3\mid u_{ij}\); (D) \(3v_{ik}-\sum_{h\le i}w_{hii}b_{hk}-\sum_{h>i}w''_{iih}b_{hk}\equiv0\) and, for \(i<j\), \(\sum_{h\le i}w_{hij}b_{hk}+\sum_{i<h\le j}w'_{ihj}b_{hk}+\sum_{h>j}w''_{ijh}b_{hk}\equiv0\pmod3\); (E) \(\sum_kv'_{ik}d_{kl}\equiv{}\)a combination of \(u\)-terms and of terms \(w_{gih}\alpha^{(gh)}_l\), \(w_{ghi}\alpha^{(gh)}_l\), \(w'_{igh}\alpha^{(gh)}_l\pmod 3\), where \(x_{2k}^3\equiv\prod_lx_{3l}^{d_{kl}}\) and \([x_g^3,x_h]\equiv\prod_lx_{3l}^{\alpha^{(gh)}_l}\pmod{\gamma_4}\); (F) \(\sum_iv_{ik}b_{ik}\equiv0\) and \(\sum_iv_{ik}b_{il}+\sum_iv_{il}b_{ik}\equiv0\pmod3\) for \(k<l\). Condition (C) is Tahara's (C) for \(p=3\) and \(d(i)=d(j)\), where \(\binom33=1\) is not divisible by \(3\); for \(p\ge5\) it is empty.

(2) Hence the \(w\)-part vanishes: for \(i\le m\) by (1) and since \(\gamma_4\) has exponent \(3\); for \(i>m\) because \(x_i^3\in\gamma_3\) and \([x_i^3,x_j,x_k]\in\gamma_5=1\). (5) With \(U\) the skew matrix \(U_{ik}=u'_{ik}\) (\(i<k\)), (B) gives \(v'_{ik}=-v_{ik}-U_{ik}\) for \(k\le m\) and \(v'_{ik}=-v_{ik}\) for \(k>m\); (F) gives \(v_{kk}\equiv0\), \(v_{lk}\equiv-v_{kl}\) for \(k,l\le m\) and \(v_{kl}\equiv0\) for \(k\le m<l\); in (E) all \(w\)-terms vanish modulo \(3\) by (1), since for a distinguished index \(g>m\) we have \(\alpha^{(gh)}\equiv0\). text: Proof. [Sketch; the case \(a=2\) is written out in Appendix B] For \(a=1\) this is Theorem 6.6; let \(a\ge2\), \(\gamma_5(Q)=1\), and let \(x_s\) have order \(3^a\) modulo \(\gamma_2\). Since \(\Lambda^2(C_{3^a}\times C_3^{s-1})\) has exponent \(3\), the factors \(\gamma_2/\gamma_3\), \(\gamma_3/\gamma_4\), \(\gamma_4\) are still elementary abelian, so identities (i)–(iii) of the proof of Theorem 6.6 hold for all \(x\in Q\), and moreover \([x^{3^n},y]=[x,y]^{3^n}\) for \(n\ge2\). The class \(x_s^{3^a}\gamma_3\) does not depend on the choice of \(x_s\), so there are two cases. If \(x_s^{3^a}\notin\gamma_3\), Tahara's (B) forces \(3\mid u_{is}\), every term involving \(x_s^{3^a}\) vanishes by the identity above, and the proof of Theorem 6.6 goes through. If \(x_s^{3^a}\in\gamma_3\), the coefficients \(u_{is}\) are unrestricted. For \(a\ge3\) all new terms are \(3^a\)-th powers of elements of \(\gamma_3\) and vanish. For \(a=2\) the new term \(\sum_iu_{is}[x_i^9,x_s]\) of \(g\) cancels only half of the pairing \(\tfrac12\sum_i[x_i^3,r_i]\), which (E) now gives as \(-\sum_iu_{is}[x_i,x_s]^9\); the remainder is \(\tfrac12[r_s^3,x_s]\) with \(r_s=\prod_ix_i^{3u_{is}}\), and condition (E) for the row \(s\), which sees \(u_{is}\) through (B) with \(d(s)/d(i)=3\), gives \(r_s^3\in\gamma_4\). So \(g=1\) for every admissible family. (This step is not void: there are groups of order \(3^{16}\) with \(x_s^9\in\gamma_3\) and \([x_i^9,x_s]\ne1\) [computer].) Theorem ([paper]). Let \(p\) be odd and \(P\) a finite \(p\)-group of class \(3\) with \(|\gamma_2(P)/\gamma_3(P)|=p^2\) and \(|\gamma_3(P)|=p\). Then \(P^{*\prime\prime}=1\). In particular every immediate descendant of step size \(1\) of \(P\) is metabelian, and \(P\) is rejected by Lemma 6.9.

Proof. \(P''\subseteq\gamma_4(P)=1\), so \(P^{*\prime\prime}\le M\), and as the subgroups \(U\) of index \(p\) in \(M\) intersect trivially it suffices to show \(Q''=1\) for \(Q=P^*/U\). Here \(\gamma_4(Q)\le\langle z\rangle\). If \(z\notin\gamma_2(Q)\), then \(\gamma_2(Q)\cong\gamma_2(P)\) is abelian. If \(z\in\gamma_2(Q)\setminus\gamma_4(Q)\), then \(\gamma_4(Q)=1\) and \(Q''\subseteq\gamma_4(Q)=1\). If \(z\in\gamma_4(Q)\), then \(Q\) has the same factors \(\gamma_2/\gamma_3\), \(\gamma_3/\gamma_4\) as \(P\), and Lemma 6.3 gives \(Q''\subseteq\gamma_5(Q)=1\). (Lemma 6.3 does not apply to \(P^*\) itself, whose lower central factors are larger.)

Remark. • For \(p=2\) the theorem fails: SmallGroup\((64,138)\) has type \((3,2,1)\), while its \(2\)-covering group has order \(2^{13}\), class \(4\) and \(|P^{*\prime\prime}|=2\); likewise SmallGroup\((128,i)\), \(i=522,599,621,1755\), and \(12\) groups of order \(2^8\) [computer]. • Check: the hypothesis holds for \(13\,315\) groups of order \(3^8\) and \(2\,754\) of order \(7^7\), and \(P^{*\prime\prime}=1\) in all of them [computer]. • The theorem does not say that such \(P\) are terminal. Of the \(7\,824\) groups of order \(3^8\) and type \((5,2,1)\) (SmallGroup\((3^8,i)\), \(1\,387\,558\le i\le1\,395\,381\)), \(190\) have nucleus of order \(3\), e.g. SmallGroup\((81,9)\times3^{1+2}_+\times C_3\), and all of their descendants are metabelian of type \((5,2,1,1)\) [computer]. For \(P/\gamma_2\) elementary abelian, nonterminality needs \(|Z(P)\cap\gamma_2(P)|=p^2\), \(\gamma_2(P)\) elementary abelian and \(P^p\le Z(P)\), and for \(p=3\) a further linear condition over \(\mathbb F_3\) [paper]; these conditions hold for the \(190\) but also for \(573\) terminal groups, and an exact criterion is open [open].

Theorem ([computer + paper]). \(D_5(Q)=\gamma_5(Q)\) for every \(3\)-group \(Q\) of order at most \(3^9\). Hence \(D_5(G)/\gamma_5(G)\) has no \(3\)-torsion for every finite group \(G\) whose Sylow \(3\)-subgroup has order at most \(3^9\).

Proof. By Theorem 5.4(3) a counterexample \(Q\) of least order has order \(3^8\) or \(3^9\), and Lemma 6.2 applies to it; for order \(3^9\) we may use the result for order \(3^8\). The deduction for \(G\) is as in Theorem 5.4.

Order \(3^8\). Every group is in the SmallGroups library (package sglppow [VLE]). Of the \(1\,396\,077\) groups, \(904\) are non-metabelian of class \(4\); all have rank \(3\) (as they must, Proposition 6.5), \(|Z|=|Q''|=|\gamma_4|=3\) and \(Q/\gamma_2\cong C_3^3\), types \((3,2,2,1)\) (\(889\)) and \((3,3,1,1)\) (\(15\)) [computer]. So Theorem 6.6 gives \(D_5=1\) for all of them. Independently, \(699\) of them have \(z\in Q''\cap M_5\), and for each the truncated Magnus algebra (\(121\) monomials, modulo \(3^{19}\), with the exactness certificate \(3^{18}\Delta\subseteq\Delta^5+3^{19}\)) gives \(z\notin D_5\) [computer].

Order \(3^9\). Let \(Q\) be a counterexample and \(P=Q/\langle zangle\), of order \(3^8\) and class \(3\) or \(4\). By Proposition 6.5(2), \(d(Q)\in\{3,4\}\); the case \(d(Q)=5\), type \((5,2,1,1)\), is excluded on paper (alternatively, by Theorem 6.10: all \(7\,824\) possible parents are rejected by Lemma 6.9, as a full run confirms). e1\) and cyclic centre, and \(62\,245\) of these have \(z\in Q''\cap M_5\). For each of the \(62\,245\) the truncated Magnus algebra gives \(z
otin D_5\), exactly. The presentations given to it were checked independently with ANUPQ (order \(3^9\), class \(4\), \(z\) central of order \(3\) in \(Q''\cap M_5\)). Let \(M=M_1\oplus M_2\oplus M_3\oplus M_4\) over \(\mathbb F_3\) with bases \(M_1=\langle e,k_1,k_2\rangle\), \(M_2=\langle u_1,u_2,\rho\rangle\), \(M_3=\langle t\rangle\), \(M_4=\langle w\rangle\), and the alternating bracket whose nonzero values on pairs of basis elements are, up to antisymmetry, \[\begin{gathered}[e,k_1]=u_1,\quad[e,k_2]=u_2,\quad[k_1,k_2]=\rho,\\ [k_1,u_2]=t,\quad[k_2,u_1]=-t,\quad[e,\rho]=-t,\quad[e,t]=w,\quad[u_1,u_2]=w.\end{gathered}\] It is graded, generated by \(M_1\), of type \((3,3,1,1)\), and \([M_2,M_2]=M_4\ne0\).

Jacobi identity [paper]. The Jacobiator \(J(x,y,z)=[[x,y],z]+[[y,z],x]+[[z,x],y]\) is alternating and trilinear and vanishes in degrees \(\ge5\), so it suffices to check triples of distinct basis elements of total degree \(3\) or \(4\). Degree \(3\): \(J(e,k_1,k_2)=[u_1,k_2]+[\rho,e]+[k_1,u_2]=t+t+t=0\), since \(3=0\) in \(\mathbb F_3\). Degree \(4\), triples \((x,y,z)\) with \(x,y\in M_1\), \(z\in M_2\): as \([k_i,t]=0\) and \([\rho,M_2]=0\), \(J(k_1,k_2,z)=[\rho,z]-[k_1,[k_2,z]]+[k_2,[k_1,z]]=0\) and \(J(e,k_i,z)=[u_i,z]-[e,[k_i,z]]+[k_i,[e,z]]=[u_i,z]-[e,[k_i,z]]\); the last two terms are both \(w\) for \((i,z)=(1,u_2)\), both \(-w\) for \((i,z)=(2,u_1)\), and both \(0\) otherwise. (A machine check of all triples agrees [computer].)

In the notation of the proof of Lemma 6.3, \(\varphi(e)=1\), \(K=\langle k_1,k_2\rangle\), \(u_i=\alpha(e,k_i)\), and \(\alpha(k_1,k_2)=\rho\ne0\) spans the radical of \(\omega\): with \(\dim M_2=3\) the form \(\omega\) may be degenerate, and the step \(\alpha(K,K)=0\) of that proof fails. The Jacobi identity for \((e,k_1,k_2)\), which there gives \(2\,\omega(u_1,u_2)=0\), here reads \(2\,\omega(u_1,u_2)=\beta(e,\rho)\), both sides being \(-1\); and it holds only because \(3t=0\), so the example is special to \(p=3\).
We write out the case \(a=2\), \(x_s^9\in\gamma_3\), of the proof of Theorem 6.8, the only case in which the new terms do not vanish by themselves. The other cases are as in the sketch.

Setting. \(Q\) is a finite \(3\)-group of class \(\le4\), \(Q/\gamma_2\cong C_9\times C_3^{s-1}\) with \(s\ge2\), and \(\gamma_i=\gamma_i(Q)\). Then \(\gamma_3\) is abelian, \(\gamma_4\) is central, \([\gamma_2,\gamma_3]=1\), \([\gamma_2,\gamma_2]\subseteq\gamma_4\), and for \(x\in Q\) the maps \(c\mapsto[c,x]\) and \(c\mapsto[x,c]\) are homomorphisms \(\gamma_3\to\gamma_4\) trivial on \(\gamma_4\).

Identities [paper]. (a) \(\gamma_2/\gamma_3\), \(\gamma_3/\gamma_4\) and \(\gamma_4\) are elementary abelian. Indeed, for a basis \(\bar x_1,\dots,\bar x_s\) of \(Q/\gamma_2\) with \(\bar x_s\) of order \(9\), \(\gamma_2/\gamma_3\) is spanned by the \([x_i,x_j]\gamma_3\), \(i<j\), where \(i<s\) and \([x_i,x_j]^3\equiv[x_i^3,x_j]\equiv1\pmod{\gamma_3}\) as \(x_i^3\in\gamma_2\); the other two factors are spanned by the values of bilinear maps whose first argument lies in the previous factor. Hence the proofs of the identities of Theorem 6.6 apply: \(\pi\colon\gamma_2/\gamma_3\to\gamma_3/\gamma_4\), \(a\mapsto a^3\gamma_4\), is a homomorphism and \((ab)^3=a^3b^3\) for \(a,b\in\gamma_2\); and identity (iii) holds for all \(x\in Q\). Moreover, by the Hall–Petrescu formula \((xy)^3\equiv x^3y^3\pmod{\gamma_3}\), so \(x\mapsto x^3\gamma_3\) is a homomorphism \(P\) from \(\Omega=\{x\in Q:x^3\in\gamma_2\}\) to \(\gamma_2/\gamma_3\), trivial on \(\gamma_2\). (b) \([x^9,y]=[x,y]^9\) for all \(x,y\in Q\). Let \(c=[x,y]\). Since \([c,x]\in\gamma_3\) commutes with \(c\) and \([c,x,x]\) is central, \([x^3,y]=c^{x^2}c^xc=c^3f\) with \(f=[c,x]^3[c,x,x]\in\gamma_4\). Put \(Z=x^3\) and \(d=[Z,y]\in\gamma_2\). By (iii), \([d,Z]=[d,x]^3\in\gamma_4\) is central, so \([x^9,y]=[Z^3,y]=d^{Z^2}d^Zd=d^3[d,Z]^3=d^3=c^9f^3=c^9\).

Basis. Let \(W=\Omega/\gamma_2\cong\mathbb F_3^s\), \(\bar P\colon W\to\gamma_2/\gamma_3\) the map induced by \(P\), \(m=\operatorname{rk}\bar P\), and \(\bar z=x_s^3\gamma_2\in W\); then \(\bar P(\bar z)=x_s^9\gamma_3=0\). Choose \(x_1,\dots,x_{s-1}\in\Omega\) such that \(\bar P(\bar x_1),\dots,\bar P(\bar x_m)\) is a basis of \(\operatorname{im}\bar P\) and \(\bar x_{m+1},\dots,\bar x_{s-1},\bar z\) is a basis of \(\ker\bar P\). Then \(\bar x_1,\dots,\bar x_{s-1}\) are independent modulo \(\langle\bar x_s\rangle\cap W=\langle\bar z\rangle\), and \(3^{s-1}\cdot9=|Q/\gamma_2|\), so \(x_1,\dots,x_s\) is a basis of uniqueness of \(Q/\gamma_2\) with \(d(i)=3\) for \(i<s\) and \(d(s)=9\). Put \(Y_i=x_i^3\) for \(i\le m\); these are independent modulo \(\gamma_3\), and we take \(x_{2k}=Y_k\) for \(k\le m\), completed to a basis of \(\gamma_2/\gamma_3\), and all \(e(k)=f(l)=3\) by (a). Then \(b_{ik}=\delta_{ik}\) for \(i\le m\), \(b_{ik}=0\) for \(m<i\le s\) (as \(x_i^3\in\gamma_3\) for \(m<i<s\) and \(x_s^9\in\gamma_3\)), and \(\zeta:=x_s^9\gamma_4=\sum_lc_{sl}\bar x_{3l}\).

Tahara's conditions. By [Tah81, Thm. 6.1], \(D_5(Q)\) is generated by the elements \[g=\sum_{i<j}u_{ij}\tfrac{d(j)}{d(i)}[x_i^{d(i)},x_j]+\sum_{i,k}v_{ik}\sum_{l>k}b_{il}[x_{2l},x_{2k}]+\sum_{i\le j\le k}w_{ijk}[x_i^{d(i)},x_j,x_k]\] over the integer families satisfying (A)–(F) (signs as in the proof of Theorem 6.6). With the orders above we use: (A) \(w_{iii}=0\); (B) for \(i<s\), \(\sum_{i<h\le s}u_{ih}b_{hk}-\sum_{h<i}u_{hi}b_{hk}+3v_{ik}+3v'_{ik}=0\), and for \(i=s\), \(-3\sum_{h<s}u_{hs}b_{hk}+9v_{sk}+3v'_{sk}=0\); (C) \(3\mid u_{ij}\) for \(i<j<s\) (for \(j=s\) it is empty, as \(3\) divides \(\binom92\) and \(\binom93\)); (D) and (F) exactly as in the proof of Theorem 6.6; and (E), modulo \(3\), \[\sum_kv'_{ik}d_{kl}\equiv\sum_{h>i}u_{ih}c_{hl}-\sum_{h<i}u_{hi}\tfrac{d(i)}{d(h)}\bigl(\alpha^{(hi)}_l+c_{hl}\bigr)-E^w_{il},\] where \(E^w_{il}\) is a sum of products of a coefficient \(w_{\cdots}\), \(w'_{\cdots}\) or \(w''_{\cdots}\) with distinguished index \(g\) and some \(\alpha^{(gh)}_l\), \(g\le h\); here \(\alpha^{(gg)}=0\), as read off Tahara's generators of types (V), (VI) [Tah81, pp. 150–151].

\(g=1\) for every admissible family. (1) As in steps (1), (2) of the proof of Theorem 6.6, (D) with \(b_{hk}=\delta_{hk}\) (\(k\le m\)) shows that \(3\) divides every \(w\)-coefficient whose distinguished index is \(\le m\). Hence the \(w\)-part of \(g\) vanishes (for \(i\le m\) by this, for \(m<i<s\) because \(x_i^3\in\gamma_3\), and for \(i=s\) only \(w_{sss}=0\) occurs), and \(E^w_{il}\equiv0\) (for \(g\le m\) by this, for \(m<g<s\) because \([x_g^3,x_h]\in\gamma_4\), and for \(g=s\) because then \(h=s\)). (2) The \(u\)-part. For \(i<j<s\), as in step (3) there, \(u_{ij}[x_i^3,x_j]=u'_{ij}[Y_i,Y_j]\) with \(u_{ij}=3u'_{ij}\), and this is \(1\) unless \(i,j\le m\). For \(j=s\) the term is \([x_i^3,x_s]^{3u_{is}}=[x_i^9,x_s]^{u_{is}}\), since \([x_i^3,x_s]^3=(c^3f)^3=c^9\) in the notation of (b); it is \(1\) for \(m<i<s\), where \(x_i^9\in\gamma_4\). (3) The \(v\)-part is \(\sum_{k<i\le m}v_{ik}[Y_i,Y_k]\). (4) For \(i\le m\), (B) and (F) give, as in step (5) there (the term \(u_{is}b_{sk}\) is \(0\)), \(v'_{ik}=-v_{ik}-U_{ik}\) for \(k\le m\) and \(v'_{ik}=-v_{ik}\) for \(k>m\), with \(U\) the skew matrix \(U_{ik}=u'_{ik}\) (\(i<k\)), and \(v_{kk}\equiv0\), \(v_{lk}\equiv-v_{kl}\) for \(k,l\le m\), \(v_{kl}\equiv0\) for \(k\le m<l\). For \(i=s\), (B) gives \(v'_{sk}=u_{ks}-3v_{sk}\) for \(k\le m\) and \(v'_{sk}=-3v_{sk}\) for \(k>m\). (5) Put \(a_i=\prod_kx_{2k}^{v'_{ik}}\in\gamma_2\), so that the left side of (E) is the coordinate vector of \(\pi(a_i\gamma_3)\). For \(i\le m\) the terms with \(h<i\) vanish modulo \(3\) by (C), and of those with \(h>i\) only \(h=s\) survives; so \(\pi(a_i)=u_{is}\zeta\). For \(i=s\) every \(u\)-term carries the factor \(d(s)/d(h)=3\), so \(\pi(a_s)=0\). Let \(M=v+U\) on indices \(\le m\) (skew with zero diagonal modulo \(3\)), \(r_i=\prod_{k\le m}Y_k^{M_{ik}}\) for \(i\le m\), and \(r_s=\prod_{i\le m}Y_i^{u_{is}}\). By (4), \(a_i\equiv r_i^{-1}\) and \(a_s\equiv r_s\pmod{\gamma_3}\); therefore \[r_i^3\equiv x_s^{-9u_{is}}\pmod{\gamma_4}\quad(i\le m),\qquad r_s^3\in\gamma_4.\] (6) Writing \(\gamma_4\) additively (exponent \(3\), so \(\tfrac12\) makes sense), \[g=\sum_{k<i\le m}M_{ik}[Y_i,Y_k]+\sum_{i\le m}u_{is}[x_i^9,x_s]=\tfrac12\sum_{i\le m}[Y_i,r_i]+\sum_{i\le m}u_{is}[x_i^9,x_s].\] By identity (iii) and (5), \([Y_i,r_i]=[x_i^3,r_i]=[x_i,r_i^3]=[x_i,x_s^9]^{-u_{is}}\), and by (b), \([x_i,x_s^9]=[x_s,x_i]^{-9}=[x_i,x_s]^9=[x_i^9,x_s]\). So the pairing cancels only half of the new term: \[g=\bigl(1-\tfrac12\bigr)\sum_{i\le m}u_{is}[x_i^9,x_s]=\tfrac12\Bigl[\prod_{i\le m}x_i^{9u_{is}},\,x_s\Bigr]=\tfrac12\,[r_s^3,x_s],\] since \(x_i^9=Y_i^3\in\gamma_3\) and \(\prod_iY_i^{3u_{is}}=r_s^3\) by (a). By (5), \(r_s^3\in\gamma_4\) is central, so \(g=1\).
